planting.note: Set divisions or container plants in spring; this species also does well planted in fall in mild-winter areas.

directions: This trailing Japanese species carries flat, rounded, blue-gray leaves in whorls of three along arching stems, forming a low mound that looks equally good spilling over a rock wall or a container rim. Clusters of small, star-shaped pink flowers open at the stem tips in early to mid fall, later than most border sedums, giving the plant a distinct season of interest. Grow in lean, fast-draining soil in full sun; too much shade or fertility produces loose, sprawling stems and fewer flowers. Established clumps need almost no attention beyond an occasional spring division to keep them tidy and vigorous.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Ruby Glow Sedum (Sprawling Wine-Red Hybrid Stonecrop)

planting.note: Set container-grown divisions in spring, spacing them to allow the sprawling stems room to spread outward.

directions: An older but still widely grown hybrid between Hylotelephium cauticola and H. telephium, Ruby Glow forms a low, sprawling mound of gray-purple foliage on trailing stems, well suited to draping over the edge of a wall or a raised bed. Deep ruby-red, star-shaped flower clusters open from late summer into fall and hold their color as they age, drawing bees and butterflies. Plant in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; rich, damp soil encourages floppy growth and weakens the naturally sturdy stems. Cut the dried flower heads back in late winter and divide congested clumps every few years to keep the display full.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Set rooted cuttings or divisions in spring; this fast-spreading groundcover fills in within a single growing season.

directions: A German-bred selection of the popular two-row stonecrop, Fuldaglut carries small, fleshy, bronze-red leaves that deepen to a rich wine color in full sun, especially through cooler spring and fall weather. Flat clusters of deep carmine-red flowers cover the mat in summer, drawing bees and small butterflies. Plant in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; it roots readily wherever a trailing stem touches soil, making it easy to fill gaps between pavers or along a rock garden edge. Shear lightly after flowering to keep the mat dense and to encourage fresh, deeply colored new growth.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: Wildfire Sedum (Burgundy Foliage with Hot Pink New Growth Sunsparkler Stonecrop)

planting.note: Set container-grown divisions in spring once soil is workable, spacing to let the mounded rosettes fill in without crowding.

directions: Wildfire is a Sunsparkler-series selection whose new leaves emerge with vivid hot-pink margins around a deep burgundy center, giving each rosette a two-toned, flame-like look that persists through the growing season before deep rose-pink flower clusters open in late summer. Grow in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; strong sun exposure and lean soil intensify the edge color, while shade or rich soil mutes it and produces looser growth. Avoid overwatering, which is the most common cause of crown rot in this and other Sunsparkler cultivars. Divide crowded clumps in spring every three to four years to maintain a tight habit.
sources: Proven Winners Sunsparkler Sedum series information

common_name: Cinco de Mayo Sedum (Color-Changing Blue-to-Coral Sunsparkler Stonecrop)

planting.note: Set container-grown divisions in spring once soil is workable, spacing to let the mounded rosettes fill in without crowding.

directions: Cinco de Mayo is a Sunsparkler-series selection grown for foliage that shifts through the season, opening powdery blue-gray in spring and warming to coral-orange and pink tones by summer's end, topped with rosy-pink flower clusters in late summer. Grow in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun, where the color transitions are most pronounced; shaded plants stay greener and change color less dramatically. Keep soil on the dry side once established, since soggy conditions are the most common cause of failure in this cultivar. Divide congested clumps in spring every three to four years to renew vigor and habit.
sources: Proven Winners Sunsparkler Sedum series information
